tasks.description: Create a `Vector` class with `x` and `y`. Implement `__str__` to print as 'Vector(x, y)' and `__repr__` to print the same.
tasks.hint:
`__str__` is for end-users: `return f'Vector({self.x}, {self.y})'`
`__repr__` is for developers/debugging — often same as `__str__` for simple classes.
Python calls `__str__` when you `print()`, `__repr__` in the REPL.
tasks.walkthrough:
`print(v)` uses `__str__`. `repr(v)` and printing a list of vectors use `__repr__`.
For a simple class both return the same thing, so they're written identically.

tasks.description: Add `__add__` to your Vector class so you can use `v1 + v2`. Test: Vector(1, 2) + Vector(3, 4) should give Vector(4, 6).
tasks.hint:
`def __add__(self, other): return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)`
This makes the `+` operator work on your objects.
Python translates `v1 + v2` into `v1.__add__(v2)` automatically.
tasks.walkthrough:
Python turns `a + b` into `a.__add__(b)`. The method builds a new Vector from the summed components.
`print` then uses `__str__` to show it as `Vector(4, 6)`.

tasks.description: Add `__len__` to return the number of components (2 for a 2D vector) and `__eq__` to compare two vectors.
tasks.hint:
`def __len__(self): return 2` — makes `len(v)` work.
`def __eq__(self, other): return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y`
Now `len(v)` and `v1 == v2` both work naturally.
tasks.walkthrough:
`__len__` returns 2 because a 2D vector has two components.
`__eq__` compares both components, so two separate objects with the same values count as equal.

tasks.description: Create a `Stack` class with `__len__`, `__bool__` (True if non-empty), and `__contains__` (for the `in` operator).
tasks.hint:
`__len__(self): return len(self._items)` — use a list internally.
`__bool__(self): return len(self) > 0` — empty stack is falsy.
`__contains__(self, item): return item in self._items` — makes `x in stack` work.
tasks.walkthrough:
The stack keeps its items in a private list and forwards the three dunders to it.
`__bool__` makes an empty stack falsy, which lets you write `while stack:` to drain it.
`__contains__` is what makes the `in` keyword work.

tasks.description: Implement `__iter__` and `__next__` on a class `Countdown` that counts down from n to 0.
tasks.hint:
`def __iter__(self): return self` — returns the iterator itself.
`def __next__(self): if self.current < 0: raise StopIteration; val = self.current; self.current -= 1; return val`
`for n in Countdown(5): print(n)` now works!
tasks.walkthrough:
`__iter__` returns the object itself, saying "I'm my own iterator".
Each `__next__` call hands out the current value and steps down. When it drops below zero, StopIteration tells the loop to end.

lesson.intro:
"Dunder" is short for double underscore. Methods like `__init__` and `__str__`
have those names because Python calls them for you at particular moments:
when an object is created, printed, added, compared, or looped over. Define
the right ones and your own classes behave like built-in types.

sections.heading: __str__ and __repr__
sections.body:
`__str__` is the friendly version, used by `print`. `__repr__` is the
developer version, used in the interactive shell and inside lists. If you
only define one, make it `__repr__`; `str` falls back to it.

sections.heading: __add__ and __eq__: operators
sections.body:
`v1 + v2` calls `v1.__add__(v2)`. `v1 == v2` calls `v1.__eq__(v2)`. Define
them and the operators work on your objects. `__add__` should return a new
object rather than changing either operand.

sections.heading: __len__, __bool__, __contains__
sections.body:
`len(obj)`, `if obj:` and `x in obj` each have a dunder behind them. A
container class that wraps a list can forward them.

sections.heading: __iter__ and __next__: making something loopable
sections.body:
A `for` loop calls `iter()` on the object, then `next()` repeatedly until
StopIteration is raised. Implement those two and your class works in a loop.

watch_out: `__str__` and `__repr__` must return strings. Printing inside them is wrong.
If you define `__eq__` without `__hash__`, objects can no longer go in sets or be dict keys. Usually fine.
`__next__` must raise StopIteration to end the loop, not return None.
